text: All performance figures of sections 1 to 14 are cross-validated estimates on the training data and none of them uses the test labels; the scores of the submitted files on the labels that the organisers released afterwards are in section 15 and were used to choose nothing. The stack AUC changes with the scored population: CYP3A4 0.7836 on all rows vs 0.8443 on confident rows, CYP2D6 0.6749 vs 0.7536. The leaderboard score of an entry is a separate measurement on the hidden labels, and the step from these estimates to it depends on the model (L2).

The official baseline scores 0.3816 (CYP3A4) and 0.1761 (CYP2D6) on the live board, well above its cross-validated score on the same data, so cross-validation under-states leaderboard performance by an amount that depends on the model; the live board scores only part of the test set.

The label rule was recovered from the data (mismatches: CYP3A4 0, CYP2D6 0). The released test labels showed that the organisers score nearly the whole test set (section 15, question 2b), so the confidence cut-off used for the cross-validated estimates scores fewer compounds than the official score does; every analysis was repeated at two cut-offs, and the estimates are those of a problem that is easier than the one that is scored.

Committee disagreement adds information beyond the decision margin for 1 components on CYP3A4 and 2 on CYP2D6 under the permutation test; where the count is zero the committee is reported as a measured negative result and does not alter predictions.

The probabilities the final build publishes (isotonic-calibrated) have calibration slopes of 0.9252 (CYP3A4) and 0.8249 (CYP2D6) on held-out folds. The sigmoid of the regularised blend as it comes out is a ranking score and not a probability (slopes 1.1813 and -0.0164); it is never published as one. Probabilities are calibrated to the weighted validation population, not to the unknown scored test population.

On the diverse crystal benchmark the model's first-pick pose is 4.1929 A from the crystal pose on average; the structure score depends on a handful of compounds and is noisy. The benchmark ligands come from the PDB, which co-folding models may have seen, so absolute accuracy is optimistic.

The test suite has 1104 passing and 0 failing tests in this run. Multi-threaded LightGBM is not guaranteed bit-identical across thread counts (see the determinism section); the pipeline fixes seeds and thread counts, and cached predictions are checked against a fresh fit.
The working tree has 0 modified and 0 untracked entries: results in this report come from uncommitted code until the work is committed.

The scored CYP2D6 set may contain many compounds the screen would never have promoted (scored as inactive). The selection-aware file gains AUC when they are numerous and loses both AUC and MCC when there are none, by more than it gains at the call rate of the final build (the table of job 016 in section 7), and neither the label-shift estimate nor the public metrics of the baseline identify their share (538 grid points are consistent with the metrics). The live board scores half of the test set and cannot separate the two files (job 016), so the entry is the hits-only file and the selection-aware file is kept, with its SHA-256, to be scored on the test labels if the organisers publish them: that comparison measures the share and tests the hypothesis on data that no choice of this project touched.

The CYP2D6 blend as it comes out is close to a constant (weighted expected calibration error 0.3592 against 0.0431 for CYP3A4): it ranks and transfers a call rate but is not a probability. The probabilities that are published pass through an isotonic step fitted on inner out-of-fold scores, which brings the error to 0.0054 (CYP2D6) and 0.0189 (CYP3A4); a monotone step restores calibration and adds no discrimination.

The CYP3A4 reaction-phenotyping and inhibition release of the laboratory that measured the challenge (Octant, same compound library) contains one compound that is also in the blinded test set (its identifier is withheld here, because the release rule forbids naming a blinded compound in a file that would be pushed). Its measurements are excluded from every use of that release and are never read by a model or a validation; the other rows of the release are used only for an independent check of the motif screen and never enter a prediction.

Two families of Chemprop candidates were run as a staged design under a rule written beforehand, for CYP3A4 only: CheMeleon was screened on 5 folds and not continued, because its gain (+0.0035 AUC) was below the bar of the stage rule, and the two OpenADMET pretraining weights (MiniMol targets and the Novartis ADMET surrogate) passed the screen and were run to the 15-fold gate, which they met. A candidate that was screened on 5 folds and not continued, or not run (CYP2D6), has no verdict: the report does not call it NOT MET, and the smallest gain that a 5-fold screen can certify is about one and a half times the smallest gain of the 15-fold design (see the design-floor figure). CYP2D6 was left out of the whole Chemprop design by a decision of 2026-10-16, taken before any CheMeleon measurement and confirmed on 2026-10-22: plain Chemprop is at chance on CYP2D6 (outer AUC 0.54 and 0.53) while the frozen CheMeleon block reaches 0.63, and the full design costs about 12 days of machine time (about 37 minutes per task, 80 tasks for each variant and enzyme) for a gain that was expected to be small: the first estimate of what the fine-tuned network could add, +0.004 to +0.008 AUC, was below the smallest difference of about 0.01 that the design can certify. The decision was taken before the result of the OpenADMET weights on CYP3A4 was known, so that whether they help on CYP2D6 is untested and not answered. The code and the weight files are in the repository.

The positive rate of the scored test set was recovered from the public leaderboards, which publish accuracy, precision and recall for every prediction file; the three numbers fix the rate (the implied rate agrees across all entries). It is aggregate information about the hidden labels that was available because the boards publish it: it weights the evaluation yardstick (the test prevalence) and sets the call rate (a multiple of the prevalence). No label of any compound and no per-compound information from a board was used, and no submission was made to probe a label. A model without this step would call the positive rate of the training data (about one fifth for both enzymes) instead of about one third (CYP3A4) and one in seventeen (CYP2D6), which costs MCC mostly on CYP2D6. A check that reads no board (a label-shift estimate from the training data and the blinded structures, `cypmode/challenge/label_shift.py`, with a rule fixed before its first run) is reported with its verdict in the innovation summary of the method report; the rate used by the final build rests on the boards.

The pocket block and the site model were tested with a conformer ensemble of 12 conformers within 5 kcal/mol of the lowest, which holds a member within 1.0 A of the crystal pose for only 12% of 131 crystal ligand copies; 300 conformers do so for 15%. Their negative verdicts are those of models that mostly did not see the bound conformation of the ligand. A wider ensemble was not tried.

On the live board, which scores 10 of the 20 ligands, the submitted structure recipe scored an LDDT-PLI of 0.3623, below the organisers' Boltz-2 baseline (0.3950), with a lower BiSyRMSD (4.3220 A against 5.1870 A). The second candidate, the first eligible unguided pose, scored 0.3975 and did not pass the threshold registered before its upload. The gates of the structure track were measured on 30 crystal ligands that are chemically far from the 20 official ligands, so the evidence for the iron-nitrogen restraint may not transfer, and no rule for choosing a pose among the predicted ones passed its gate. The recipe is reported as submitted and makes no claim of a better LDDT-PLI than the baseline.

The ligand dynamics in the frozen pocket ran 20 ps for each of 104 predicted poses of 10 benchmark ligands, with the protein and the heme held at their predicted positions and without water. It is not a dynophore of the literature, which follows the whole complex in water over nanoseconds, and it cannot show that a pose is wrong because the pocket would open, that a bridging water molecule is missing, or that a slow motion of the ligand changes the pose. The stability of a pose measures its agreement with the force field that also relaxed it. 0 of its three scores met the gate registered before the result (the highest mean rho was +0.042 against the bar of +0.30); 10 ligands cannot detect a modest effect, so the result is that this cheap dynamics did not rank the predicted poses of these ligands and says nothing about a dynamics of the whole complex or about the 20 official ligands, which are chemically far from the benchmark ligands.
